---
title: "Bounded responses"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

A slider response recorded between zero and one gives us three pieces of measurement information. First, values below zero and above one are impossible. Second, a participant may deliberately select either endpoint. Third, the available spread shrinks near an endpoint: a mean near zero leaves much more room above it than below it. We should preserve all three facts when choosing a response model.

We use the **MegaNegRaising** data described by [An and White (2020)](https://aclanthology.org/2020.scil-1.45/) and the accompanying [project documentation](https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-negraising/).

The conditional [variance and standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) describe response spread on the chosen slider scale. A [residual](residuals.qmd) is observed minus fitted response, so its possible values also depend on the endpoints and fitted mean.

The MegaNegRaising sliders put observations at both boundaries and change their spread across fitted locations. Defining the two prompts and the balanced subset makes those empirical failures of a Gaussian benchmark interpretable.

Each raw row contains paired judgments: how likely matrix negation conveys embedded negation and how easy it is to imagine someone uttering the matrix-negated sentence. An and White call the ease response acceptability while noting the simplification. The experiment had already restricted which predicate and frame combinations were eligible on the basis of earlier acceptability evidence. Our current subset then adds a different set of restrictions: native speakers of American English, eventive infinitivals in the past tense and active or passive voice, first- and third-person subjects, and verbs represented in all four combinations of voice and subject.

The balancing step uses the participant, predicate, frame, voice, and subject labels. It never inspects either slider value. In particular, no trial is removed because the ease judgment is high or low.

The first slider targets the **neg raising inference**: how strongly a sentence with matrix negation supports interpreting the embedded proposition as negated. The second records how easy it is to imagine someone producing that sentence. The prepared table scales both responses to $[0,1]$, with zero and one as selectable endpoints. The balanced extract omits sentence text and the original verbal endpoint labels, so we do not reconstruct either. The linked paper and project documentation remain the source for the complete prompt.

```{r}
#| label: load-meganegraising-bounds
#| echo: true
mnr <- read.csv("data/meganegraising/meganegraising-balanced.csv")
mnr$voice <- factor(mnr$voice, levels = c("active", "passive"))
mnr$subject <- factor(mnr$subject, levels = c("first", "third"))
stopifnot(nrow(mnr) == 7651L, length(unique(mnr$participant)) == 1091L,
          length(unique(mnr$verb)) == 193L)
c(rows = nrow(mnr), participants = length(unique(mnr$participant)),
  verbs = length(unique(mnr$verb)))
slider_bounds <- range(c(mnr$negraising, mnr$acceptability))
summary_table <- data.frame(
  response = c("neg-raising", "ease"),
  mean = c(mean(mnr$negraising), mean(mnr$acceptability)),
  zero_probability = c(mean(mnr$negraising == slider_bounds[[1L]]),
                       mean(mnr$acceptability == slider_bounds[[1L]])),
  one_probability = c(mean(mnr$negraising == slider_bounds[[2L]]),
                      mean(mnr$acceptability == slider_bounds[[2L]])),
  endpoint_probability = c(mean(mnr$negraising %in% c(0, 1)),
                           mean(mnr$acceptability %in% c(0, 1)))
)
summary_table
```

One actual retained response is:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-meganegraising-row
mnr[1L, c(
  "participant", "verb", "frame", "voice", "subject", "negraising",
  "acceptability"
)]
```

This row retains one participant's paired measurement. No averaging to a verb mean has occurred. `frame`, `voice`, and `subject` identify the sentence template; `negraising` and `acceptability` are the two recorded slider locations. Requiring every retained verb to occur in all four combinations of voice and subject supports those contrasts while narrowing the analysis to the eligible predicates that satisfy the current crossing restriction.

An ordinary Gaussian model assigns positive probability outside the response support. We fit the neg-raising benchmark with participant and verb intercepts, then calculate that illegal probability from its fitted population means and residual standard deviation.

```{r}
#| label: gaussian-bounded-benchmark
#| echo: true
gaussian <- lme4::lmer(
  negraising ~ voice * subject + (1 | participant) + (1 | verb),
  data = mnr, REML = FALSE,
  control = lme4::lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa",
                              optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L))
)
mnr$gaussian_mean <- predict(gaussian, re.form = NA)
sigma_hat <- sigma(gaussian)
mnr$illegal_probability <- pnorm(0, mnr$gaussian_mean, sigma_hat) +
  pnorm(1, mnr$gaussian_mean, sigma_hat, lower.tail = FALSE)
c(fixed_effects = lme4::fixef(gaussian),
  average_illegal_probability = mean(mnr$illegal_probability))
```

For a fitted Gaussian mean $\widehat\mu_i$ and residual SD $\widehat\sigma$, the illegal predictive mass for row $i$ is

$$
\Phi\left(\frac{0-\widehat\mu_i}{\widehat\sigma}\right)
+
1-
\Phi\left(\frac{1-\widehat\mu_i}{\widehat\sigma}\right).
$$

The code computes these two tails with `pnorm()` and then averages them across fitted population means. We call the resulting mismatch the **endpoint mass problem**. The Gaussian curve extends beyond the legal response range, assigning positive probability to impossible values, while every exact endpoint receives probability zero.

```{r}
#| label: plot-bounded-responses
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
density_grid <- data.frame(value = seq(-.2, 1.2, length.out = 301L))
density_grid$fitted_density <- vapply(
  density_grid$value,
  function(value) mean(dnorm(value, mnr$gaussian_mean, sigma_hat)),
  numeric(1)
)
ggplot(mnr, aes(negraising)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = .05, boundary = 0,
                 color = "white", fill = "grey55") +
  geom_line(data = density_grid, aes(value, fitted_density),
            color = "#1F5A85", linewidth = .8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = slider_bounds, color = "grey65", linewidth = .4) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = range(density_grid$value)) +
  labs(x = "Neg-raising slider response", y = "Density") +
  theme_classic()
```

The Gaussian benchmark assigns `r scales::percent(mean(mnr$illegal_probability), accuracy = .01)` of its predictive mass outside $[0,1]$. Participants could select the endpoints, and the endpoint bars record those selections directly.

The source paper uses the ease response to weight a measure of how far the model's predicted response distribution is from the observed judgments. That calculation belongs to a latent lexical and structural model with participant-specific scale and shift terms. The analysis here does not use ease to remove or retain trials: it asks only whether the Gaussian benchmark assigns probability to impossible slider values. Reproducing the source analysis would require its latent structure and weighting procedure.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why is an exact response of zero different from a small positive response?
2. Which probability does the Gaussian benchmark assign to an exact endpoint?
3. What population restriction is introduced by retaining verbs in all four cells?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The measurement procedure allows respondents to select zero exactly. We therefore retain zero rather than treating it as an approximation to an interior value. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. A continuous Gaussian assigns probability zero to any exact point, including zero and one, while also assigning positive mass outside the legal interval. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. The target is limited first by the experiment's predicate and frame eligibility criteria and then by the current restrictions on native speaker status, tense, frame, person, and representation in all four conditions. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>

We next ask why [ordinary beta regression](why-not-beta-sliders.qmd) still cannot represent the endpoint observations.
